analogy.p: Think of a non-renewable resource as a **savings account** that nobody pays into: every time you withdraw from it the balance falls, and eventually it hits zero. A renewable resource is like a **well fed by a spring**, which refills as you take water from it. The analogy breaks down because some renewable sources (such as wind and sunshine) cannot be stored, so you cannot take them out later like water, and a well can still run dry if you use it too fast.
analogy.t: A bank account and a well

bullets: The resources to know: **coal, oil, gas, nuclear fuel, biofuel, wind, hydroelectricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun (solar) and water waves**.
**Transport:** petrol, diesel and kerosene come from oil; biofuels can replace some of these; electric vehicles use electricity generated from any of the resources.
**Electricity generation:** most resources can drive turbines and generators; solar cells make electricity directly.
**Heating:** gas for central heating and cooking, coal and wood for fires, solar water heating panels, and electricity for heaters.
Fossil fuels and nuclear fuel are **fuels** that are burned or reacted to release energy; the others use natural energy flows.
Electricity is **not** an energy resource itself, it is a way to transfer energy that is made using a resource.
A single resource often serves more than one use (gas heats homes and generates electricity).
core.h: Energy resources and what they are used for
core.p: An **energy resource** is a source from which we can obtain energy to do useful things. The AQA specification lists the main energy resources available on Earth: **fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, biofuel, wind, hydroelectricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves**. These resources are used in three main ways: **transport**, **electricity generation** and **heating**. You need to be able to describe the main uses of each resource and classify it as renewable or non-renewable.

bullets: **Non-renewable:** coal, oil, natural gas (the fossil fuels) and nuclear fuel (uranium and plutonium).
**Renewable:** biofuel, wind, hydroelectricity, geothermal, tides, the Sun (solar) and water waves.
Fossil fuels took **millions of years** to form from the remains of dead plants and animals, so they cannot be replaced on a human timescale.
Renewable does **not** mean unlimited output at any time; for example, there is not always wind or sunshine.
Biofuels are renewable because new plants can be grown to replace those used.
Nuclear fuel is non-renewable because the supply of uranium ore on Earth is finite.
Saying 'renewable resources never run out' is acceptable at a basic level but the better answer is 'they are replenished as they are used'.
core.p: The key distinction is whether the resource can be replaced on a human timescale. A **renewable** energy resource is one that is **being (or can be) replenished as it is used**. A **non-renewable** energy resource is one that **will run out**, because it is not replaced as quickly as it is used. Examiners reward the idea of **replenished** (renewable) and **will run out** (non-renewable) so use those words.

bullets: **Formation:** from the remains of ancient plants and animals over millions of years.
**Burning** releases energy and produces **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas that contributes to **global warming** and climate change.
Burning coal and oil can release **sulfur dioxide**, which causes **acid rain**.
Burning fuels can release **particulates** (soot) and **nitrogen oxides**, harming health and causing global dimming.
**Advantages:** reliable, can be started when needed, relatively cheap to run, existing infrastructure.
**Disadvantages:** non-renewable, emit pollutants, mining and drilling damage the environment, oil spills are possible.
Gas power stations start up faster and emit less carbon dioxide per unit of energy than coal.
core.h: Fossil fuels: coal, oil and gas
core.p: Fossil fuels are the main resource used in the UK for electricity, heating and transport. They are burned to release energy from the chemical energy store, and in a power station that energy is used to heat water to make steam, which turns a turbine connected to a generator. Their big advantages are that they are reliable, on demand and have a high energy output, while the disadvantages are that they are non-renewable and release carbon dioxide when burned.

bullets: Chain: chemical energy store (fuel) → thermal energy → kinetic energy of steam → kinetic energy of turbine → electrical energy.
The steam is **cooled and condensed** back into water and is reused.
Not all energy is transferred usefully: much is wasted as thermal energy, so the efficiency is well below 100%.
The generator works by electromagnetic induction (a coil rotating in a magnetic field).
In **nuclear** stations, energy is released by **nuclear fission** of uranium or plutonium in a reactor to heat water.
The output of a fuel power station can be **increased or decreased** to match demand, which is why they are called reliable.
Wind, hydroelectric, wave and tidal power use the movement of the resource to turn the turbine directly (no boiler needed).
core.h: How a fuel-burning power station works
core.p: Most of the electricity in the UK is produced by a similar chain of energy transfers. The fuel (coal, oil, gas or biofuel) is burned in a boiler to heat water, producing high-pressure **steam**. The steam is directed at the blades of a **turbine**, making it rotate. The turbine turns a **generator**, which produces electricity, and that is sent to the **National Grid**. Nuclear power stations use the same turbine and generator but the heat source is nuclear fission.

bullets: **Fuel:** uranium and plutonium (non-renewable).
**Advantages:** no greenhouse gases from the process, reliable, very large energy output from a small amount of fuel.
**Disadvantages:** radioactive waste needs safe storage for a long time, accident risks, high building and decommissioning cost.
They take a long time to start up and are less able to meet sudden changes in demand than gas.
Nuclear power stations are used to give a steady base amount of electricity.
Public concern about safety and waste affects whether new stations are built.
Fission is covered in more detail in the atomic structure and radioactivity topics.
core.p: Nuclear power stations use the energy released when atoms of uranium or plutonium undergo **fission**. The fuel is non-renewable but a very small mass releases a huge amount of energy. A major benefit is that no carbon dioxide is released by the reaction itself, so it does not contribute to the greenhouse effect. The main drawbacks are the **radioactive waste**, which stays dangerous for a very long time and must be stored safely, the risk of accidents, and the very high cost of building and decommissioning the stations.

bullets: Examples: **ethanol** (from fermenting sugar), **biodiesel** (from plant oils), **biogas** (methane from decaying waste), wood.
**Advantages:** renewable, can be carbon neutral over their lifetime, can use waste, can replace petrol and diesel in vehicles.
**Disadvantages:** need large areas of land, which can compete with food crops or cause habitat loss and deforestation.
Burning biofuels still releases carbon dioxide, but plants take it back in as they grow.
Producing, harvesting and transporting biofuel crops uses energy, which usually comes from fossil fuels.
Biofuel supply depends on growing seasons and weather, but it can be stored, so it is reliable on demand.
Cost is often higher than for fossil fuels, and engines may need to be adapted.
core.p: **Biofuels** are fuels made from plant or animal waste, such as ethanol made from sugar crops or biogas produced from rotting waste. They can be burned for electricity generation, heating, or as transport fuels. They are renewable because crops can be regrown, and they can be nearly **carbon neutral**, as the carbon dioxide released when burned was absorbed by the plants while they grew. However, growing them needs land, which can reduce food production or lead to deforestation.

bullets: Energy transfer: kinetic energy of wind → kinetic energy of blades → electrical energy.
**Advantages:** renewable, no fuel cost, no pollution while running, can be built at sea (offshore) and on land.
**Disadvantages:** unreliable because it depends on wind, **cannot** increase output on demand, visual and noise impact, harm to birds.
Initial cost of building is high, but running costs are low.
Offshore wind farms have stronger and steadier winds but cost more to build and maintain.
Wind is a good example of a resource where reliability depends on the weather.
A calm day gives little or no electricity, so other sources must make up the demand.
core.p: Wind turbines use the **kinetic energy of moving air** to turn blades, which rotate a generator directly. They produce no carbon dioxide while operating and have no fuel costs. They only work when the wind is blowing at a suitable speed, so the output is variable and cannot be increased on demand. Many people dislike how they look and the noise they make, and they can affect birds and bats.

bullets: Hydroelectric: gravitational potential energy of water → kinetic energy → turbine → generator → electricity.
**Hydroelectric advantages:** renewable, quick to start up so useful for meeting sudden demand, no fuel needed, no greenhouse gases in operation.
**Hydroelectric disadvantages:** flooding of valleys destroys habitats and can displace people, expensive to build, needs suitable hilly area and rainfall.
**Tidal advantages:** predictable (tides occur twice a day at known times), renewable, no pollution when running.
**Tidal disadvantages:** barrages change the estuary habitat, affect wading birds and ships, high building cost, output varies through the cycle, not available everywhere.
Tidal power is reliable in the sense of being predictable, but the amount of energy changes over the month.
Water waves differ from the tides: waves are caused by wind blowing over the sea surface.
core.p: **Hydroelectric** power uses water stored behind a dam. When released, the water flows downhill through pipes and turns turbines, transferring gravitational potential energy to kinetic energy and then electrical energy. **Tidal** power uses the rise and fall of the tides: a **tidal barrage** across an estuary lets water through turbines as the tide comes in and goes out. Tides are very predictable but the barrage can damage habitats.

bullets: **Wave:** kinetic energy of waves → generator; renewable, no pollution; unreliable and may harm marine life; hard to maintain.
**Geothermal:** thermal energy from hot rocks heats water to steam; reliable, little pollution, can supply heating directly.
Geothermal is only available in certain places, and drilling is expensive.
**Solar cells** produce electricity directly from sunlight, with no moving parts; useful for remote places and calculators.
Solar output depends on daylight and cloud, and no electricity is made at night.
Solar cells have a high initial cost but low running costs, and no pollution when in use.
Solar water heating panels use the Sun's energy to heat water for homes.
core.p: **Wave power** uses the up-and-down motion of sea waves to drive generators, but the supply varies with the weather and the equipment is difficult to maintain in rough seas. **Geothermal** power uses hot rocks underground: water is pumped down, heated into steam, and returned to the surface to turn a turbine. This is only practical in places with hot rocks near the surface, such as Iceland. **Solar** energy from the Sun can be captured by **solar cells**, which transfer light directly to electricity, or by solar panels that heat water.

bullets: **Reliable on demand:** fossil fuels, nuclear, biofuel, hydroelectric (from stored water), geothermal.
**Dependent on weather or time:** wind, solar, waves; tides are predictable but vary over a month.
**Low carbon dioxide in operation:** nuclear and all renewables (biofuels are carbon neutral over time).
**High carbon dioxide:** coal, then oil, then gas (gas is the lowest of the three).
**Habitat damage:** hydroelectric dams, tidal barrages, biofuel land use, mining and drilling.
**Cost:** renewables often have high set-up costs but low running costs; nuclear has very high set-up and decommissioning costs.
**Location:** geothermal, hydroelectric and tidal need suitable sites; solar and wind work in many places.
The ability to be switched on quickly matters for meeting peaks in demand.
core.h: Comparing the resources: advantages and disadvantages
core.p: A typical exam question asks you to evaluate or compare two resources, so you should organise your knowledge by themes: **reliability**, **environmental impact**, **cost**, **how quickly output can be changed**, and **where it can be used**. Fossil fuels and nuclear are usually reliable but non-renewable, whereas most renewables are low in emissions but depend on the weather, tides or location. A good answer always compares like with like and gives a reasoned judgement.

bullets: Reasons for increased use of renewables: reduce carbon dioxide emissions, fossil fuels will run out, technology getting cheaper, government policy.
Reasons for slower change: renewables can be unreliable, high set-up costs, need for new power lines, people object to wind farms in their area.
Changing from coal to gas cuts emissions, because gas releases less carbon dioxide for the same energy.
Demand for electricity rises as population grows and as more devices (such as electric vehicles) are used.
Transport still depends heavily on oil-based fuels, though electric vehicles and biofuels are growing.
Energy resources' use varies by country depending on what natural resources the country has (such as hills for hydroelectric power).
When reading data, describe the **overall pattern** and use figures from the table or graph.
core.h: Trends in the use of energy resources
core.p: The specification asks you to explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources. Over recent decades the UK and many other countries have moved away from coal and towards natural gas, and have increased the use of renewable resources such as wind and solar. Reasons include concern about **climate change** and the greenhouse effect, government **targets and subsidies**, falling costs of renewable technology, and the knowledge that fossil fuels will eventually run out. Trends are limited by reliability, cost and the need for new infrastructure.

bullets: Use the structure: **name → how it works → advantage → disadvantage** for any resource you are asked about.
Link renewable resources to reduced use of fossil fuels and lower greenhouse gas emissions.
Link to the **energy stores and transfers** from earlier: chemical, nuclear, gravitational potential, kinetic, thermal, electrical.
Link to **efficiency**: all power stations that use steam waste a lot as thermal energy.
For decision questions, give both sides before a conclusion.
Explain **why** a resource is renewable or not, not just state it.
Higher-level answers refer to **reliability, cost and environmental impact** together.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam application
core.p: This topic links to **efficiency** (a more efficient device needs less fuel), to **electricity and the National Grid** (power stations feed into it), to **atomic structure** (nuclear fission), and to **climate change** in other sciences (carbon dioxide and the greenhouse effect). The next spec point compares reliability, cost and environmental impact in more depth, so make sure your descriptions of each resource include the energy transfer, one advantage and one disadvantage.

exam: **State (1 mark):** give a definition, e.g. 'a renewable resource is one that is being replenished as it is used'.
**Give/name (1 mark):** list resources accurately: renewables are biofuel, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, tides, solar and waves.
**Describe how electricity is generated (3 to 4 marks):** fuel heats water → steam → turns turbine → turns generator; mention the energy transfers.
**Advantage/disadvantage (2 marks):** make sure the point is specific to the resource (e.g. wind is unreliable) rather than a generic comment like 'it is bad'.
**Compare (4 marks):** write about both resources on the same criterion (reliability, cost, environment), using words like 'whereas' or 'however'.
**Evaluate/6 marks:** consider reliability, cost and environmental impact, give both sides, and finish with a justified conclusion.
**Data questions:** state the trend, quote figures from the table or graph, and calculate percentages if asked (part ÷ whole × 100).
**Explain trends:** link to reasons such as climate change targets, reduced cost of technology, and the running out of fossil fuels.
**Be precise with terms:** use 'replenished', 'on demand', 'greenhouse gas', and 'carbon dioxide' rather than vague words like 'pollution' only.
**Command words:** 'Suggest' means apply knowledge to a new case; 'Explain' needs a 'because'.
**Spelling:** biofuel, geothermal, hydroelectric and turbine are commonly misspelt and can be penalised in extended answers.

mistakes.w: Renewable means it never runs out.

mistakes.r: Nuclear fuel (uranium/plutonium) is non-renewable; it produces no carbon dioxide but the fuel is finite.
mistakes.w: Nuclear power is renewable because it is clean.

mistakes.r: They release carbon dioxide when burned, but plants absorbed it while growing, so they can be carbon neutral.
mistakes.w: Biofuels do not produce carbon dioxide.

mistakes.r: They only work when there is enough wind, so the output is unreliable and cannot be increased on demand.
mistakes.w: Wind turbines work all the time.

mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide causes global warming; sulfur dioxide causes acid rain.
mistakes.w: Fossil fuels cause acid rain because of carbon dioxide.

mistakes.r: Electricity is a way of transferring energy; resources are used to generate it.
Solar cells transfer light to electricity; solar water heating panels heat water.
Tides are caused by the Moon and Sun's gravity and are predictable; waves are caused by wind on the sea.
mistakes.w: Tidal and wave power are the same.

mistakes.r: Building a dam floods valleys and destroys habitats.
mistakes.w: Hydroelectric power has no environmental impact.

summary: You must know the main energy resources (fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, biofuel, wind, hydroelectricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves), their uses in transport, electricity generation and heating, and be able to distinguish renewable from non-renewable resources. It matters because choosing a resource involves trade-offs in reliability, cost and environmental impact.

terms.d: A source from which energy can be obtained to provide a useful transfer.
An energy resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
An energy resource that will run out because it is not replaced as quickly as it is used.
Coal, oil or gas formed over millions of years from the remains of dead plants and animals.
Uranium or plutonium, whose nuclei release energy in nuclear fission.
A fuel made from plant or animal waste.
Electricity generated by water falling through turbines, usually from a dam.
Energy obtained from hot rocks below the Earth's surface.
A dam across an estuary that uses the rise and fall of the tide to turn turbines.
A device that transfers light energy directly into electrical energy.
A set of blades that rotates when a fluid such as steam, wind or water passes over it.
A device that transfers kinetic energy into electrical energy.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide, that absorbs thermal radiation and contributes to global warming.
Releasing no net carbon dioxide because the carbon dioxide released equals that taken in.
Able to supply energy whenever it is needed.

worked.ans: A renewable resource is replenished as it is used, for example wind, whereas a non-renewable resource will run out because it is used faster than it forms, for example natural gas.
worked.q: Explain the difference between a renewable and a non-renewable energy resource and give one example of each. (4 marks)
steps: Define renewable: a resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
Example of renewable: wind (or solar, tides, hydroelectric).
Define non-renewable: a resource that will run out because it is not replaced as quickly as it is used.
Example of non-renewable: coal, oil, gas or nuclear fuel.

worked.q: A country generates 300 TWh of electricity in a year, of which 120 TWh comes from renewable resources. Calculate the percentage from renewables and the percentage from non-renewable sources. (3 marks)

worked.ans: Gas is burned to heat water into steam; the steam rotates a turbine, which turns a generator to produce electricity; the steam is condensed and reused, and some energy is wasted as thermal energy.
worked.q: Describe how electricity is generated in a gas-fired power station. (4 marks)
steps: The gas is burned in a boiler, transferring energy from the chemical store.
This heats water to produce steam.
The turbine drives a generator, which produces electricity.
